items.prompt: Per this unit, what is "expected value" (EV)?
choices: The most likely single outcome of a decision
The probability-weighted average of every possible outcome's value
The best-case outcome, ignoring probability entirely
The average of the probabilities themselves, ignoring the values
items.reference: 🧮 EV = Σ (probability × value)
items.explanation: Expected value is the probability-weighted average of every possible outcome's value — each outcome counted in proportion to how often it would happen if the decision were repeated many times.

items.prompt: Which everyday idea is expected value closest to, per this unit?
choices: A guess about what will happen the very next time
The average outcome you'd see if you could replay the same risky decision an enormous number of times
A rule that guarantees the best possible outcome every time
A measure of how confident you feel about a decision
items.reference: 🧮 EV = Σ (probability × value)
items.explanation: EV is the average outcome you'd see if you could replay the same risky decision an enormous number of times — a long-run average, not a forecast of any single attempt.

items.prompt: In the phrase "probability-weighted average," what does "weighted" mean here?
choices: Every outcome counts equally, regardless of how likely it is
Each outcome's contribution to the average is scaled by how likely it is to happen
Only the heaviest (largest-magnitude) outcome counts
Weighting is unrelated to probability in this context
items.reference: 🧮 EV = Σ (probability × value)
items.explanation: "Weighted" means each outcome's value is scaled by its probability before being added in — a 1%-likely outcome contributes far less to the average than a 50%-likely one, even if their raw values are similar.

items.prompt: Which formula matches this unit's definition of expected value across a set of outcomes?
choices: EV = probability of the best outcome only
EV = sum of (probability of each outcome × value of that outcome)
EV = sum of all values, divided by the number of outcomes
EV = the highest value among all possible outcomes
items.reference: 🧮 EV = (p₁×v₁) + (p₂×v₂) + ...
items.explanation: EV is the sum, across every outcome, of that outcome's probability multiplied by its value — not a simple average of the raw values, and not just the best or most likely outcome alone.

items.prompt: What must be true of a decision's outcome probabilities before you can trust the EV computed from them?
choices: They must all be equal to each other
They must add up to 1 across all the mutually exclusive outcomes
They must all be greater than 50%
There must be exactly two outcomes
items.reference: 🧮 EV = (p₁×v₁) + (p₂×v₂) + ...
items.explanation: The probabilities for one decision's mutually exclusive, collectively exhaustive outcomes must sum to 1 — otherwise the "average" being computed isn't actually an average of anything real.

items.prompt: In the opening scenario, what is the expected value of migrating today?
items.reference:
⚡ Migrate now: 0.15×(−50000) + 0.85×8000 = −$700
🌙 Wait: 0.02×(−50000) + 0.98×5000 = +$3,900
items.explanation: Migrating today has EV = 0.15 × (−$50,000) + 0.85 × $8,000 = −$700 — a negative expected value, despite the 85% chance of a positive outcome, because the 15% failure branch is so costly.

items.prompt: In the opening scenario, what is the expected value of waiting for the maintenance window?
items.reference:
⚡ Migrate now: 0.15×(−50000) + 0.85×8000 = −$700
🌙 Wait: 0.02×(−50000) + 0.98×5000 = +$3,900
items.explanation: Waiting has EV = 0.02 × (−$50,000) + 0.98 × $5,000 = +$3,900 — the lower outage probability and the guaranteed success payoff outweigh the extra coordination cost baked into the smaller $5,000 success value.

items.prompt: Roughly how much more is waiting for the window worth, on average, than migrating today, per the opening scenario's numbers?
choices: About $700 more
About $4,600 more
They're worth exactly the same
Migrating today is worth more, by about $700
items.reference:
⚡ Migrate now: 0.15×(−50000) + 0.85×8000 = −$700
🌙 Wait: 0.02×(−50000) + 0.98×5000 = +$3,900
items.explanation: The gap is $3,900 − (−$700) = $4,600 — waiting is worth about $4,600 more on average, which is exactly the number the arithmetic reveals that "2% feels safer than 15%" alone does not.

items.prompt: If EV(migrate now) = −$700, does that mean today's migration will actually lose exactly $700?
choices: Yes, EV is a precise prediction of this one attempt
No — the actual outcome will be either −$50,000 or +$8,000, never exactly −$700; EV is a long-run average, not a single-attempt forecast
No, because the calculation itself must be wrong if it doesn't match a real outcome
Yes, but only if the migration is run more than once
items.reference:
🚫 EV is not a single-attempt forecast
📈 It's a long-run average across many repeats
items.explanation: EV(now) = −$700 will never actually happen as an outcome — the migration either succeeds (+$8,000) or fails (−$50,000). EV describes the average across many hypothetical repeats, not a prediction of this specific attempt.

items.prompt: According to this unit, when does a team's EV-positive decision-making strategy pay off most reliably?
choices: On the very first decision it's applied to
Consistently, across many similar decisions made over time — not necessarily on any single decision
Never — EV has no practical value
Only when every decision happens to succeed
items.reference:
🚫 EV is not a single-attempt forecast
📈 It's a long-run average across many repeats
items.explanation: A team that consistently makes EV-positive calls comes out ahead over a year of many decisions, even though any individual decision can still go the "wrong" way — EV is about the long run, not any single roll.

items.prompt: In the opening scenario, why isn't "2% is obviously safer than 15%, just wait" a complete answer on its own?
choices: Because it compares probabilities alone without weighing what's actually at stake in each outcome
Because 2% is actually higher than 15%
Because probabilities are never useful for decisions
Because the scenario doesn't specify any probabilities at all
items.reference:
❌ "Safer" ≠ "worth more on average"
✅ Weigh probability AND payoff together
items.explanation: Comparing 2% and 15% alone answers "which is safer," not "which choice is worth more on average" — that second question requires weighing each probability against its actual payoff, which is what expected value does.

items.prompt: What's the core reason this unit gives for computing expected value instead of relying on gut feel?
choices: Gut feel is always wrong
It lets you weigh the size of a risk against the size of its reward with an actual number, instead of comparing feelings about probabilities alone
Numbers are inherently more trustworthy than any other kind of reasoning
It removes the need to ever think about probability again
items.reference:
❌ "Safer" ≠ "worth more on average"
✅ Weigh probability AND payoff together
items.explanation: The point isn't that gut feel is worthless — it's that weighing probability against payoff with an actual number surfaces conclusions (like waiting being worth $4,600 more) that a comparison of percentages alone can miss.

items.prompt: Per this unit, which single number correctly answers "which option is worth more on average" in the opening scenario?
choices: The probability of failure alone (15% vs. 2%)
The expected value of each option, computed from both probability and payoff together
The size of the worst-case loss alone ($50,000 for both)
The size of the best-case gain alone ($8,000 vs. $5,000)
items.reference:
❌ "Safer" ≠ "worth more on average"
✅ Weigh probability AND payoff together
items.explanation: Looking at probability alone, payoff alone, or worst-case alone each misses part of the picture — only expected value, which combines probability and payoff for every outcome, actually answers "which option is worth more on average."

items.prompt: Per L2's decision tree, what shape of node represents a choice you control, versus one you don't?
choices: Square nodes for choices you control; circular "chance" nodes for outcomes you don't
Circular nodes for choices; square nodes for chance
Both choices and chance outcomes use the same node shape
Triangle nodes for choices; circle nodes for chance
items.reference:
◻️ Square = decision node (you choose)
⭕ Circle = chance node (probability decides)
items.explanation: L2's tree uses square nodes for decision points ("migrate now or wait?", a choice under your control) and circular chance nodes for the probabilistic outcomes beneath each choice.

items.prompt: Why must a chance node's outgoing branch probabilities sum to exactly 1, per L2?
choices: It's just a stylistic convention with no real consequence
Because that constraint is what makes "the average outcome" a well-defined number rather than an arbitrary weighted guess
It only matters for chance nodes with more than two branches
Probabilities summing to 1 is optional as long as the values are correct
items.reference:
◻️ Square = decision node (you choose)
⭕ Circle = chance node (probability decides)
items.explanation: L2 is explicit that the sum-to-1 constraint isn't decoration — without it, the weighted sum computed from the branches isn't a well-defined average of anything real, which is exactly why both L3 code functions raise an error if it's violated.

items.prompt: Per L2, how do you evaluate a decision node once every chance node beneath it has an EV?
choices: Average all the options' EVs together
Take the best (highest) EV among the options beneath it
Always pick the option with the lowest probability of failure, regardless of EV
Decision nodes cannot be evaluated numerically
items.reference:
◻️ Square = decision node (you choose)
⭕ Circle = chance node (probability decides)
items.explanation: L2 states that evaluating a decision node means computing the EV of every branch beneath it and taking the best one — the migration decision picks "wait for window" because $3,900 beats −$700.

items.prompt: Per L2's node-by-node table, what is the sum for the "migrate now" chance node?
items.reference:
Migrate now0.15×(−50000) + 0.85×8000−700
Wait0.02×(−50000) + 0.98×5000+3900
items.explanation: The "migrate now" chance node evaluates to 0.15 × (−50,000) + 0.85 × 8,000 = −7,500 + 6,800 = −700 — multiply each branch's probability by its payoff, then add.

items.prompt: L2 says computing EV top-down means "a tree with three sequential decisions evaluates the same way, from the bottom up." What does "bottom up" mean here?
choices: Solve the leaves and deepest nodes first, then treat each solved sub-tree as a single number feeding the node above it
Start from the top-level decision and guess which branch looks best without computing anything
Evaluate every node simultaneously in one step, regardless of depth
It means the tree must be redrawn upside down before evaluating
items.reference:
Migrate now0.15×(−50000) + 0.85×8000−700
Wait0.02×(−50000) + 0.98×5000+3900
items.explanation: "Bottom up" means solving the deepest nodes (leaves and the chance nodes closest to them) first, then treating each already-solved sub-tree as a single number that feeds into the evaluation of the node above it — the same rule applied recursively at every depth.

items.prompt: Per L2's node-by-node table, what is the sum for the "wait for window" chance node?
items.reference:
Migrate now0.15×(−50000) + 0.85×8000−700
Wait0.02×(−50000) + 0.98×5000+3900
items.explanation: The "wait for window" chance node evaluates to 0.02 × (−50,000) + 0.98 × 5,000 = −1,000 + 4,900 = 3,900 — the lower failure probability and the still-positive success value combine to a solidly positive EV.

items.prompt: Per L2, does adding a deeper level to the tree (e.g. a further decision after a successful migration) make the evaluation rule more complicated?
choices: Yes, a fundamentally new rule is needed for every additional level of depth
No — each node only ever needs the numbers directly beneath it, so the same rule applies regardless of how deep the tree grows
Yes, because probabilities can no longer sum to 1 once the tree has more than two levels
The unit doesn't address trees deeper than one level
items.reference:
Migrate now0.15×(−50000) + 0.85×8000−700
Wait0.02×(−50000) + 0.98×5000+3900
items.explanation: L2 is explicit that the rule doesn't get more complicated as the tree grows deeper — each node only ever needs the numbers directly beneath it, which is what lets a bottom-up evaluation handle any depth of tree with the same simple rule.

items.prompt: Per L2, in what situation can the higher-EV option still be the wrong call?
choices: Never — the higher-EV option is always correct in every situation
When a single outcome could be catastrophic and unrecoverable, especially for a one-shot decision without a cash cushion to absorb it
Whenever the lower-EV option happens to have a lower probability of failure
Only when the two options have exactly equal EV
items.reference:
💥 A single catastrophic, unrecoverable outcome
1️⃣ A one-shot decision, not a repeated bet
items.explanation: L2's correction applies specifically when a single outcome could be catastrophic and unrecoverable — a company without the cash to survive the worst branch, facing a decision it only gets to make once, should weigh that tail risk on top of the average, not just follow the higher EV blindly.

items.prompt: Per L2, does the existential-risk correction mean expected value should be thrown out as a decision tool?
choices: Yes, EV is fundamentally unreliable and should never be trusted
No — EV is still the right first number to compute; the correction only narrows in on cases with catastrophic, unrecoverable tail risk
Yes, but only for decisions involving money
No, the correction only applies to decisions with more than two options
items.reference:
💥 A single catastrophic, unrecoverable outcome
1️⃣ A one-shot decision, not a repeated bet
items.explanation: L2 is explicit that this isn't a reason to throw out expected value — it's still the right first number to compute in most repeated decisions. The correction is narrow: check the size of the worst branch when it could be catastrophic and unrecoverable.

items.prompt: Per L2's worked example, a startup with $55,000 in the bank faces the migration decision (both options can hit a $50,000 outage). What does the existential-risk correction actually argue for here?
choices: Choosing "migrate now" instead, because it has a smaller worst case
Choosing "wait for window" — which already has the better EV *and* the much smaller (2% vs. 15%) chance of the outcome the company can't survive
Ignoring both options' EV entirely and flipping a coin
The correction doesn't apply here because neither option is actually risky
items.reference:
💥 A single catastrophic, unrecoverable outcome
1️⃣ A one-shot decision, not a repeated bet
items.explanation: L2's worked example shows the correction reinforcing the higher-EV choice here, not overriding it — waiting already has the better EV and the much smaller chance of the shared catastrophic outcome, so this is the ordinary case, not an exception.

items.prompt: Per L2's bar chart, comparing the two options' EV, which is higher and by roughly how much?
choices: "Migrate now" is higher, by about $4,600
"Wait for window" is higher, by about $4,600
They're exactly equal
"Migrate now" is higher, by about $700
items.reference:
📊 Migrate now: −$700
📊 Wait: +$3,900
items.explanation: L2's bar chart shows "wait for window" at +$3,900 versus "migrate now" at −$700 — a gap of about $4,600, visually reinforcing the same conclusion the node-by-node table computed.

items.prompt: In L2's bar chart, why does "migrate now" end up negative even though it succeeds 85% of the time?
choices: Because the chart is displaying the failure probability directly, not EV
Because the 15% chance of a $50,000 loss outweighs the 85% chance of an $8,000 gain, once weighted by their respective probabilities
Because negative bars always represent the more likely outcome
The chart contains an error — a mostly-successful option can never have negative EV
items.reference:
📊 Migrate now: −$700
📊 Wait: +$3,900
items.explanation: Even at 85% success, the 15% failure branch's $50,000 loss is large enough relative to the $8,000 gain that the weighted sum comes out negative — a high success rate alone doesn't guarantee positive EV if the failure cost is disproportionately large.

items.prompt: What single fact does L2's chart and node-by-node table both make visible that a simple 15%-vs-2% comparison hides?
choices: That the two options actually have identical probabilities
That weighing probability against payoff together flips which option looks better compared to weighing probability alone
That probabilities are irrelevant to the final decision
That the $50,000 outage cost is different for each option
items.reference:
📊 Migrate now: −$700
📊 Wait: +$3,900
items.explanation: Both visuals make the same point: weighing probability against payoff (not probability alone) is what surfaces the full $4,600 gap between the two options — a fact a bare 15%-vs-2% comparison never reveals on its own.

items.prompt: Implement `expectedValue(outcomes)`, where `outcomes` is an array of `{ probability, value }` objects. Return the probability-weighted sum of the values. You may assume probabilities already sum to 1 (no need to validate).

tests.description: matches the migration scenario's 'migrate now' EV
matches the migration scenario's 'wait for window' EV
works with three outcomes, not just two
tests.expr: expect(expectedValue([{ probability: 0.5, value: 100 }, { probability: 0.3, value: 0 }, { probability: 0.2, value: -50 }])).toBe(40)

items.explanation: expectedValue reduces the outcome list to a single number by multiplying each outcome's probability by its value and summing — exactly the arithmetic L1 and L2 walked through by hand, now as a reusable function that works for any number of outcomes.
items.reference: 🧮 EV = Σ (probability × value)

items.prompt: Implement `expectedCost(outcomes)`, where `outcomes` is an array of `{ chance, cost }` objects (`cost` can be negative, meaning a gain). Return the chance-weighted sum of the costs. You may assume the chances already sum to 1.

tests.description: matches the migration scenario's 'migrate now' EV (cost sign convention)
matches the migration scenario's 'wait for window' EV (cost sign convention)
works with three outcomes, not just two
tests.expr: expect(expectedCost([{ chance: 0.5, cost: -100 }, { chance: 0.3, cost: 0 }, { chance: 0.2, cost: 50 }])).toBe(-40)

items.explanation: expectedCost is the same weighted-sum arithmetic as expectedValue, just with the sign convention flipped (cost instead of value) — a positive expected cost means the option is worse than break-even on average, matching expectedValue's negative EV for the same numbers.
items.reference: 🧮 EV = Σ (probability × value)

items.prompt: Implement `evaluateChance(branches)`, where `branches` is an array of `{ probability, value }` (all leaves — no nested nodes). Return the chance node's expected value: the sum of probability * value across all branches. This is the building block `evaluateNode` uses for a `type: "chance"` node whose branches are all leaves.

tests.description: matches the 'wait for window' chance node

tests.expr: expect(evaluateChance([{ probability: 0.6, value: 2000 }, { probability: 0.3, value: -1000 }, { probability: 0.1, value: -4000 }])).toBe(500)

items.explanation: This is L3's evaluateNode logic for the 'chance' case, isolated to just leaf branches — the recursive version in L3 additionally handles a branch whose value comes from a nested node instead of a plain number, by resolving that nested node first.
items.reference:
⭕ Chance node EV = Σ (branch probability × branch value)
◻️ Decision node EV = best option's EV

items.prompt: Implement `pickBestOption(options)`, where `options` is an array of `{ label, ev }` objects (already-computed EVs, no need to evaluate anything). Return the `label` of the option with the highest `ev`.

tests.expr: expect(pickBestOption([{ label: 'migrate now', ev: -700 }, { label: 'wait for window', ev: 3900 }])).toBe('wait for window')

tests.description: picks correctly when the best option is first in the list

tests.expr: expect(pickBestOption([{ label: 'a', ev: 10 }, { label: 'b', ev: 999 }, { label: 'c', ev: 500 }])).toBe('b')

items.explanation: This is L3's evaluateNode logic for the 'decision' case, isolated from the recursive evaluation — once every option's EV is known, picking the best one is a plain max-by-ev reduction, the same rule L2 described as 'take the best EV among the options beneath it.'
items.reference:
⭕ Chance node EV = Σ (branch probability × branch value)
◻️ Decision node EV = best option's EV

items.prompt: Implement `sampleOutcome(outcomes, roll)`, where `outcomes` is an array of `{ probability, value }` and `roll` is a number in `[0, 1)` (already generated — no randomness needed inside this function). Walk the outcomes accumulating probability, and return the `value` of the first outcome whose cumulative probability exceeds `roll`.

tests.description: a low roll lands in the first (smaller-probability) outcome
a high roll lands in the second outcome

tests.expr: expect(sampleOutcome([{ probability: 0.2, value: 1 }, { probability: 0.3, value: 2 }, { probability: 0.5, value: 3 }], 0.45)).toBe(2)

items.explanation: sampleOutcome walks the outcome list accumulating probability mass until the roll lands inside one outcome's slice — the same idea as a spinner divided into unequal wedges, one wedge per outcome, sized by its probability. This is the core operation L3's Monte Carlo simulation repeats thousands of times to build up an empirical average.
items.reference:
🎡 Roll lands in a wedge sized by probability
📉 Empirical EV = average of many sampled outcomes

items.prompt: Implement `averageOf(values)`, where `values` is a non-empty array of numbers (e.g. sampled outcomes from many simulated trials). Return their arithmetic mean.

tests.description: averages a small set of sampled outcomes
handles a larger, evenly split set

items.explanation: This is the final step of L3's monteCarloEV: after sampling one outcome per simulated trial, averaging the whole list of sampled outcomes is what produces the empirical EV estimate that gets compared against the closed-form analytic value.
items.reference:
🎡 Roll lands in a wedge sized by probability
📉 Empirical EV = average of many sampled outcomes

items.prompt: Per L3's convergence table, was the 1,000-trial run closer to the analytic EV than the 100-trial run?
choices: Yes, larger trial counts always beat smaller ones exactly in order
No — the 1,000-trial run (−1338) was actually further from −700 than the 100-trial run (−700, an exact match by luck), showing convergence isn't perfectly monotonic
The table doesn't include a 1,000-trial run
Both runs were identical
items.reference:
100 trials−700
1,000 trials−1338
100,000 trials−756.84

Why: the law of large numbers shrinks the typical gap, not every individual run.
items.explanation: L3's table shows the 100-trial run landing exactly on −700 (a lucky draw) while the 1,000-trial run landed further away at −1338 — the law of large numbers promises the typical size of the gap shrinks as trials grow, not that every larger run beats every smaller one.

items.prompt: Per L3, what does the law of large numbers actually guarantee about Monte Carlo simulations?
choices: That any single run, no matter how small, will exactly match the analytic value
That the typical size of the gap between simulated and analytic values shrinks as the number of trials grows
That simulated values will always be higher than analytic values
Nothing useful — Monte Carlo simulation results are essentially random noise
items.reference:
100 trials−700
1,000 trials−1338
100,000 trials−756.84

Why: the law of large numbers shrinks the typical gap, not every individual run.
items.explanation: The law of large numbers guarantees the typical (not every single) gap between the sample average and the true expected value shrinks as sample size grows — which is exactly what the 100,000-trial row demonstrates, landing much closer to the analytic value than either smaller run.

items.prompt: At 100,000 trials, L3's simulation for 'migrate now' landed at −756.84 versus an analytic −700. What does this small remaining gap indicate?
choices: A bug in expectedValue() or evaluateNode()
Ordinary sampling variance from a finite (not infinite) number of trials — not a bug
That the analytic formula must be recalculated
That the seed value 1 is invalid and should never be reused
items.reference:
100 trials−700
1,000 trials−1338
100,000 trials−756.84

Why: the law of large numbers shrinks the typical gap, not every individual run.
items.explanation: Even 100,000 trials is finite, so a small remaining gap between simulated and analytic values is expected sampling variance, not evidence of a bug — a truly infinite simulation would converge exactly, but no real simulation ever runs infinitely many trials.

items.prompt: Per L3's failure-modes table, why do expectedValue() and evaluateNode() both check that probabilities sum to 1?
choices: Purely as a stylistic convention with no functional purpose
Because a typo'd probability list can silently produce a confidently wrong EV instead of raising an error, so the check catches that failure mode immediately
Because JavaScript requires this check to run at all
The functions in L3 don't actually perform this check
items.reference:
⚠️ A typo'd probability list fails silently without a check
⚠️ Small samples are noisy in both directions
items.explanation: L3's failure-modes table flags this directly: without the sum-to-1 check, a typo'd probability list (e.g. 0.15 and 0.80 instead of 0.85) would silently produce a confidently wrong EV — the check turns that into an immediate, loud error instead.

items.prompt: Per L3's failure-modes table, what does a decision-tree evaluator's "best option" fail to account for on its own?
choices: Nothing — the evaluator's chosen option is always the objectively correct final answer
The tail-risk judgment from L2 — evaluateNode() only optimizes for the highest average, with no concept of a branch that could bankrupt the company
The evaluator cannot compute EV correctly for any tree deeper than one level
The evaluator ignores probabilities entirely
items.reference:
⚠️ A typo'd probability list fails silently without a check
⚠️ Small samples are noisy in both directions
items.explanation: L3's failure-modes table is explicit that evaluateNode() only ever optimizes for the highest average EV — it has no built-in concept of catastrophic, unrecoverable risk, which is exactly the separate judgment L2 said still has to happen on top of the raw numbers.

items.prompt: Per L3's failure-modes table, does reusing the same random seed across simulation runs make a result more statistically trustworthy?
choices: Yes, a fixed seed makes the result more statistically valid
No — a fixed seed only makes results reproducible for demonstration and debugging; real confidence comes from running many different seeds and checking they agree
Yes, but only for trial counts above 10,000
Seeds have no effect on Monte Carlo simulation results at all
items.reference:
⚠️ A typo'd probability list fails silently without a check
⚠️ Small samples are noisy in both directions
items.explanation: L3 is explicit that a fixed seed exists for reproducibility (so an example can be checked and replayed), not statistical validity — genuine confidence in a Monte Carlo result comes from running many different seeds and confirming they agree, not from one seed producing a plausible-looking number.

items.prompt: Per L3's closing section, does matching the analytic EV prove the migration decision's probabilities and payoffs (15%, 2%, $50,000, etc.) are themselves accurate?
choices: Yes, a matching simulation proves the input numbers are correct
No — Monte Carlo only confirms the math correctly follows from the inputs as stated; it says nothing about whether those inputs are accurate estimates of the real world
Yes, but only if the simulation runs at least 1,000,000 trials
The unit doesn't address this question
items.reference:
✅ Confirms: the math follows correctly from the inputs
❌ Doesn't confirm: that the inputs are true
items.explanation: L3 is explicit: "garbage probabilities in, confidently wrong EV out" — a simulation matching the analytic value only confirms internal consistency between the formula and the stated inputs, never that those inputs (15%, $50,000, and so on) reflect reality.

items.prompt: L3's closing question asks what happens if migrating now, on failure, tends to cost $70,000 instead of $50,000 (waiting's failure cost stays at $50,000). Recomputing EV(now) = 0.15 × (−70000) + 0.85 × 8000, what's the new value, and does it flip the decision?
choices: New EV(now) = −3700; still worse than waiting's +3900, so the decision doesn't flip — waiting's advantage just grows
New EV(now) = +3700; this flips the decision to favor migrating now
New EV(now) = −700, unchanged from before
The new EV cannot be computed without also changing the waiting option's numbers
items.reference:
✅ Confirms: the math follows correctly from the inputs
❌ Doesn't confirm: that the inputs are true
items.explanation: 0.15 × (−70,000) + 0.85 × 8,000 = −10,500 + 6,800 = −3,700 — worse than the original −700, and still far below waiting's +3,900. A higher failure cost for 'migrate now' doesn't flip the decision here; it just widens waiting's already-existing advantage, since the same 15% failure probability now applies to an even larger loss.
